name: Daria Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a workday like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, play violin at weddings and a care-home music hour, record string parts, and teach five private pupils. I have a music bachelor’s and years of playing, but I still practise the quiet passages before anyone arrives. Watching a care-home resident hum with me is the hour I carry home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the calendar mean for your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner sells flowers, our children are grown, and the mortgage is nearly halfway paid. Four months of expenses are saved, my fees are ordinary for violin work, and a few other groups hire nearby. I use AI now and then to draft a wedding timetable, but I check the names and set times myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the wedding organiser that a faster timetable is welcome if the player fee and rehearsal call stay written. I would still ask who is paying for an extra song.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The care-home contract and five pupils give me steady weeks, and four months saved covers an ordinary cancelled wedding. I still count travel and the mortgage before saying yes to a new date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I would keep the paid care-home hour, pupils and booked weddings, and get written fees for extra songs and cancellations. In the plateau’s first year I would request an actual pension estimate and compare it with the mortgage, rather than set a retirement date from a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next season because our regular work pays. A tidy timetable is useful, but a signed player fee is what goes in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which term has caused trouble before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An extra song at a wedding once ran past the agreed finish. I would ask for its fee before carrying the violin case back in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a pension statement make you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would see the actual number beside our bills first. I have not set a retirement date.

I would welcome a **faster timetable** for booked weddings.
think: The **care-home contract** and five paid pupils make this season steadier than my variable wedding dates.
Our **four-month reserve** covers an ordinary wedding cancellation while mortgage and travel bills continue.
do: Keep **care-home music**, five paid pupils and booked weddings this winter.
Request **written extra-song fees** and cancellation terms before new dates.
Request an **actual pension estimate** in the plateau’s first year and compare it with mortgage bills.
feel: I feel **calm** about regular paid work.
S0.quote: A tidy timetable is useful, but a signed player fee is what goes in the bank.

steps.text: Keep paid care-home hour, five pupils and booked weddings this winter
Request written extra-song and cancellation fees before new wedding dates
Request actual pension estimate in first plateau year; compare with mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the wedding band that generated string parts may be cheap, but someone still has to play live when the couple walks in. I would ask which arrangements and rehearsal hours remain paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a quarter of my fees come from recording string arrangements for the bands. I expect some of those orders to fall, though the care-home hour and pupils would still pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask for written arrangement and rehearsal rates, plus a paid colleague demonstration of the school’s new score checker. In disruption’s first year I would try it only on my own nameless violin passage if the school approves local storage, play every suggested note against the printed score, and stop if a note is wrong or the file leaves the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing arrangement income that helps pay our bills. I can check a printed score, but I cannot make a band buy a recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you upload a pupil’s playing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Their names and performances stay in the school folder. My own little passage is enough for the trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the colleague has no paid hour to teach it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I keep using paper and my ears. I would not take unpaid instruction to save the school money.

I would remind the band **live violin** matters at the ceremony.

feel: I feel **anxious** about plausible arrangement losses.
S1.quote: I can check a printed score, but I cannot make a band buy a recording.
fieldNote: The **new checker** needs paid demonstration, approved local storage, owned nameless music and manual violin checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that thinking AGI in 2028 could make string arrangements before a robot can play a wedding around 2031. I would ask the couple’s planner to sign the live player fee now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recorded arrangements bring about a quarter of my pay, and I expect most recording orders to stop in 2028. If the band also cuts live calls, the care-home and pupil work alone may not cover our usual bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total my arrangement invoices and get written wedding and care-home dates. In the first year after 2028, if recording orders end and live wedding calls also fall, I would apply for a posted paid care-home music tutor job only if its requirements accept my music degree and years teaching pupils, its written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees and the bus home runs; I would keep current paid calls and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the likely recording loss, though the four-month reserve gives us some time to find paid work. I would be alarmed if the weddings disappeared as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a care-home tutor rather than a booking desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A human tutor can hear when a resident is tired and change the music in the room. I have done that in our paid weekly hour, but a posted employer still has to accept my qualifications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When could a playing robot matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card puts capable hands-on robots around 2031. My recorded parts can lose their price in 2028, so I will check the earlier contract first.

I would separate **2028 AGI** from robot wedding players around 2031.
think: Recordings bring a **quarter of my pay**, and I expect most orders to stop in 2028.

feel: I feel **anxious** about likely recording loss, with some reserve to search.
S2.quote: A human tutor can hear when a resident is tired and change the music in the room.
fieldNote: The **2028 loss** reaches recorded arrangements before robot violin playing around 2031.
Her **tutor option** involves human listening and needs a posted paid role accepting her degree and pupil teaching.

steps.text: Total recording invoices and request written wedding/care-home dates now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the music centre that five years until AGI by 2031 is time to test a paid violin circle for adults. I would say a real bow teacher and safe instruments need real fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arrangements may thin before 2031, and a small group could replace some of that work. Four months saved means I can test interest, but I will not pay a room and assistant out of the mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would ask for written room hire before taking fees, and keep the care-home call and five pupils while I test a six-week adult violin circle. I would start only when seven adults prepay enough for my teaching and preparation, a paid bow assistant, room, inspected instrument hire and travel; after 2031 I would renew only at the same full seven-place floor, replacing unsafe violins or deferring and refunding the whole group if seven safe paid places cannot remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the possible arrangement cut, but a fully paid circle would give me another route. Seven paid violin places must carry the room, both workers and the trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only five people enrol?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refund all five and keep the paid work already in the calendar. Five fees do not cover the room and two workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when a hired violin is unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would find a safe replacement before anyone plays. If that leaves fewer than seven safe paid places, I would defer and refund the whole group.

I would say **safe instruments** and paid bow help belong in its price.

feel: I feel **anxious** about arrangement losses while checking a funded alternative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that a decade until AGI by 2036 lets us write down player, teaching and preparation fees. Robot violin players around 2039 are later than the contracts we sign now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer late weddings, but I do not know our pension figures. Recordings could fade before 2036; the care-home hour and pupils give me something human to keep offering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request an actual pension estimate and written care-home renewal, then save one tenth of any extra paid wedding fee after mortgage, food and travel toward six months of expenses. Over the decade I would start the adult violin circle only after written room hire and seven safe paid places cover my teaching and preparation, bow-assistant wage, room, inspected instruments and travel. In the first year after 2036 I would renew on that same floor while keeping the care-home hour and pupils, replacing unsafe violins or deferring and refunding the whole group below seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant loss because present teaching and wedding work still pays. I do not count an unbooked class or an unknown pension as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no extra wedding fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then nothing new goes to the reserve from weddings. Six months is a target, not an amount we already hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire when you see the pension estimate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We would put the actual number next to the bills and my health before deciding anything. I have no set retirement date.

Start **adult violin circle** with written room, seven safe fees covering room/own teaching/preparation/assistant/hire/travel; renew after 2036 on same floor or defer/refund everyone.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant recording changes while present paid hours hold.
S4.quote: I do not count an unbooked class or an unknown pension as income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because most recorded arrangements could stop before another paid term replaces them. Written live dates, a real care-home tutor vacancy accepting my music degree and a net offer after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the bow assistant gets paid to stay until the last beginner packs up. A class is not viable just because seven people hand over fees.

headlineQuote: A class is not viable just because seven people hand over fees.
portrait: Daria is a **58-year-old violinist** with a music degree, wedding work, five pupils and a care-home hour.
Her **four-month reserve**, typical pay and some nearby groups steady present work but leave arrangement fees exposed.
She uses **AI occasionally** and tests a new score checker only with paid instruction, approved storage and manual playing.
Her **adult violin circle** needs seven safe prepaid places covering her teaching and preparation, assistant, room, hire and travel.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could end recorded arrangements before another paid term replaces them.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **written live dates**, a real tutor vacancy accepting her degree and written replacement net pay after travel.
